newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Erbakan reminds Greeks of defeats.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Erbakan reminds Greeks of defeats.

text.p: Turkish Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan on Tuesday warned Greece and the Cypriot government against a military buildup on Cyprus, reviving memories of past conflict between Turks and Greeks.
His warning was issued amid a furore over the planned deployment by Cyprus of a Russian-made S-300 missile system, which Turkey last week threatened to destroy.

Erbakan called on Cyprus to scrap plans to deploy the missiles, which could also strike planes in Turkish air space. Cyprus has said it will not bring in any part of the missile system for at least 16 months.
"It is wrong to turn Cyprus into a barrel of gunpowder. I hope Greece and Greek Cyprus give up these intolerable provocations and get smart," Erbakan said.

"The Greeks know us very well and have experience on this subject. They saw the results of what they tried to do in 1922 and 1974. I hope history does not repeat itself," he told members of his Islamist Welfare Party in parliament.

Erbakan was referring to two events in the long history of conflict between the Turks and Greeks. In 1922, Turkish troops expelled a Greek army that had invaded Anatolia during the chaos of the Ottoman Empire's collapse after World War One.
In 1974, Turkey invaded Cyprus in response to a shortlived coup in Nicosia engineered by the military then ruling Greece.

Turkey's invasion resulted in the island's division and establishment of a breakaway Turkish Cypriot state in the north recognised only by Ankara. About 30,000 Turkish troops are still stationed in Cyprus.
The United States sent an envoy to Cyprus this week to try to calm the dispute, which has raised international concern about the risk of armed conflict between Turkey and Greece.
The two neighbours, both NATO members, almost came to blows last year over ownership of two uninhabited islets in the Aegean Sea.
